candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.locator: chapter one, after the Oxbridge luncheon and the Fernham dinner (Hogarth Press, 1929)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Before any large thanks can be meant there is the small one, that somebody fed you, and that the day starts from a body which was looked after.

candidates.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
candidates.author: Rabindranath Tagore
candidates.whyThisMonth: It holds the month’s two subjects in one breath: a short life, and enough of it, which is the only arithmetic gratitude ever needs.

candidates.quote: Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.locator: to Fanny Keats, Winchester, 28 August 1819, p. 285 (ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man with very little time left writes out the list of what he wants, and every item on it is ordinary, cheap and already within reach.

candidates.quote: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the spaces between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
candidates.author: Maya Angelou
candidates.work: Singin’ and Swingin’ and Gettin’ Merry Like Christmas
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the thing that carried her and thanks it by name, which is what gratitude looks like when it is a debt rather than a mood.

candidates.quote: Let them a journey new begin, / But I at last with weary feet / Will turn towards the lighted inn, / My evening-rest and sleep to meet.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: Book VI, chapter 6, Many Partings (George Allen and Unwin, 1955)
candidates.speaker: Bilbo Baggins
candidates.whyThisMonth: The gentlest picture of an ending in English, not a cliff but a lit window at the end of a long walk, and a reader can carry it all day.

candidates.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
candidates.author: Horace
candidates.locator: Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5, p. 279 (trans. C. E. Bennett, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man who knows he will die says plainly what he made and lets the work stand in for the life, which is one honest answer to the month.

candidates.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
candidates.author: William Blake
candidates.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
candidates.whyThisMonth: It turns the fact that things pass into the reason they are loved, so a reader wakes to a world worth having because it will not keep.

candidates.quote: You only live twice: / Once when you are born / And once when you look death in the face.
candidates.author: Ian Fleming
candidates.locator: the epigraph, printed as after Bashō (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts the second birth exactly where the month wants it, in the plain look at the end, in three lines a tired reader can hold.

candidates.quote: Do not go gentle into that good night, / Old age should burn and rave at close of day; / Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
candidates.author: Dylan Thomas
candidates.work: Do not go gentle into that good night
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 3, In Country Sleep and Other Poems (New Directions, 1952)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the one famous line about last things that asks for more heat rather than less, and at six in the morning that is the useful direction.

candidates.quote: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
candidates.author: Heraclitus
candidates.locator: fragments 41 and 42, in Early Greek Philosophy, 2nd edition (trans. John Burnet, 1908)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest way of saying that nothing waits, said so calmly that it reads as an invitation to look at this morning rather than as a warning.

candidates.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
candidates.author: Italo Calvino
candidates.locator: the sixth of the fourteen definitions (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A quiet argument that some made things outlive their makers and go on talking, which is the consoling half of a month about last things.

candidates.quote: A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.work: The Old Man and the Sea
candidates.locator: p. 103, the words Santiago says aloud on the way home (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1952)
candidates.speaker: Santiago
candidates.whyThisMonth: It separates what can be taken from a person from what cannot, which is the distinction a reader needs on a morning about endings.

candidates.quote: Last, loneliest, loveliest, exquisite, apart— / On us, on us the unswerving season smiles, / Who wonder ’mid our fern why men depart / To seek the Happy Isles!
candidates.author: Rudyard Kipling
candidates.locator: the Auckland stanza, The Seven Seas (Methuen, 1896)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four lines of a place thanking its own weather and wondering why anyone would leave it to go looking elsewhere for the blessed islands.

candidates.quote: The trees are in their autumn beauty, / The woodland paths are dry, / Under the October twilight the water / Mirrors a still sky; / Upon the brimming water among the stones / Are nine-and-fifty swans.
candidates.author: W. B. Yeats
candidates.locator: the opening stanza, The Wild Swans at Coole (Macmillan, 1919)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It counts what is still there on an autumn morning, from a poem that goes on to count the years, so beauty and passing arrive together.

candidates.quote: Whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul . . . then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.
candidates.author: Herman Melville
candidates.locator: chapter 1, Loomings, the middle clauses elided (Harper and Brothers, 1851)
candidates.speaker: Ishmael
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives the month’s own grey mood a name and a remedy in the same breath, which is more use at six than either of the two alone.

candidates.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
candidates.locator: chapter III, Napa Wine, the clause raised to a sentence (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five words of thanks for a year of sun held in a bottle, which is the harvest half of the month said as briefly as it can be said.
